extracted.intended_audience: educated readers interested in manners, taste, and social conduct (gentlemen and ladies of early-18th-century English society)
extracted.subtask_description: A periodical essay giving prescriptive guidance and moral observation about personal conduct, breeding, dress, conversation, clergy behaviour, and the management of servants. The piece illustrates standards by character sketches and anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and Plainness
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity and Plainness (the old English plainness and honesty of disposition) are preferable to hollow compliment and affected manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincerity argues true greatness of mind, is accompanied by courage and resolution, and is better than mere show. When speech becomes empty compliment, 'Words are like Money' but often mere cyphers; language 'running into a Lie' makes most conversation a trade of dissimulation and breeds weariness of the world. Be plain and sincere rather than counterfeit; being what you seem is the best way to seem anything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑artifice: consequences of dissimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Artifice and dissimulation bring perpetual inconvenience because they produce jealousy, suspicion, and loss of reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False appearances may yield short convenience but long-term harm: when a man forfeits the reputation of integrity, 'he is set fast, and nothing will then serve his Turn, neither Truth nor Falshood.' Therefore avoid practices that risk undermining trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum (Regard to Decency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decorum — a regard to decency — is closely related to virtue and should govern dress, speech, and behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decency appears in order, consistency, and moderation of words and actions; it carries deference to the good opinion of others and earns respect. To be negligent of what others think shows arrogance or abandonment. Distinguish virtues: as justice avoids violence, modesty avoids committing offence — that avoidance is the force of decency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate female dress and behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Women should dress and behave so as to recommend themselves in the social characters of sister, daughter, or wife, remaining 'what Nature designed them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adopting masculine or romantick hunting habits ill-suited to English modesty (e.g., the Amazonian hunting-habit). Such imitations break the propriety and the distinct beauty of different characters; maintain the natural agreeableness of sex by being themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turning public assemblies into masquerade
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining propriety of appearance preserves the beauty of different social characters; frequent mixtures of dress that blur sex distinctions would make assemblies a masquerade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the fashions that confuse distinctions became common, public gatherings would lose the clear forms by which characters are recognized; therefore preserve proper distinctions of dress and carriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion in conversation — know your depth
rubrics_metrics.description: One should have the discretion not to go beyond one’s depth in conversation; apparent knowledge is preferable to exposed ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The socially adept (e.g., Will Honeycomb) shine where they keep within their depth; those who cannot converse outside their profession or sphere are 'pedants' of a different sort. It is better to appear to know than to display glaring ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being a mere specialist/pedant
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who knows only the matters of his profession or particular way of life (a 'mere' anything) is a pedant and a poor companion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand thinking beyond one's profession: mere courtier, soldier, scholar, lawyer, or man of the town — each limited to a narrow circle of accomplishments — are equally ridiculous. True learning should be joined with common sense and taste; otherwise learning makes a silly man insufferable by supplying matter to his impertinence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning should cultivate good sense and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning, like travelling, ought to finish and improve good sense; without taste and distinction it can produce vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware those who have 'read a great number of Books without Taste or Distinction.' Shallow pedants lavish praise on one another for trivial editorial acts; real education should produce wisdom and humility, not arrogance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergyman: prefer elocution and plain sense over laboured composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Country clergy should aim for graceful delivery, a good aspect, clear voice, and plain sense rather than elaborate original compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sermon 'repeated after this manner' (well delivered) is like a poet's composition in the mouth of a graceful actor; it is more edifying and easier for clergy to adopt the works of better masters and focus on handsome elocution and delivery to enforce the written text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergyman: pastoral temper and dedication to parish welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: A good parish clergyman is sociable, of regular life, practical in divinity, and devoted to his parishioners' welfare without self-seeking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualities admired: plain sense, obliging conversation, regular life, charitable action (preventing lawsuits, dispensing justice), and arranging practical sermons as a continued system of practical divinity. Reward and long-term provision for such men are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masterly treatment of servants: benevolence and prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: The corruption of servants' manners arises from bad masters; a good master governs with humanity, equal temper, and prudent economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating servants with respect, rewarding them appropriately, keeping faithful long-term servants, and not habitually dressing them in cast clothes (which creates a false sense of equality) produce industry, cheerfulness, and loyalty. Orders should be received as favours rather than burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewarding and advancing servants appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: A good master secures the future of faithful servants by giving them opportunities for independent livelihood (apprenticeships, settlements) rather than merely small trinkets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frugality enables generosity: rather than giving cast cloaths, help a good servant to leave servitude by providing settlements or paying fines for apprenticeship; such manumission encourages the next servant to be diligent and humble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value long service and show public appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Long service merits public recognition and preferential treatment (affection, rewards, fulfillment of promises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir Roger's household shows affectionate regard for long-serving domestics (tears at arrival, pressing to help, secret concern at infirmity). Honor past service materially (land, annuity, or other settlement) and publicly acknowledge devotion (portraits, stories) to encourage fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal small industriousness and obliging civility (Will Wimble model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A likeable country gentleman makes and gives small useful things, maintains pleasant correspondence, and performs obliging attentions to neighbours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be handy in harmless handicrafts (making flies, nets, garters), exchange small tokens (tulip-roots, poppies), offer practical help (bring lash for a whip), and keep cheerful sociability; these little arts endear one to the community.
